---
title: "Quiz: convolutional networks"
---

Short questions on convolutional layers, pooling, receptive fields and augmentation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A convolutional layer with $C_\text{out}$ kernels of size $k \times k$ on $C_\text{in}$ channels has $k^2C_\text{in}C_\text{out} + C_\text{out}$ weights; output size $\lfloor(n + 2p - k)/s\rfloor + 1$.

---

**Q1.** A convolutional layer has 32 kernels of size $3 \times 3$ on an RGB image. How many weights does it have? How many for a $256 \times 256$ image, and for a $2048 \times 2048$ image?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each kernel covers all 3 channels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 32 + 32 = 896$, for both image sizes: the same kernels are used at every position.
:::

---

**Q2.** The input is shifted 5 pixels to the right. What happens to the feature maps of a convolutional layer (stride 1)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Equivariance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
They shift 5 pixels to the right as well (apart from the border columns): the same kernel sees the same neighbourhoods, now 5 pixels further right.
:::

---

**Q3.** A $64 \times 64$ feature map goes through 2×2 max pooling, then a $3 \times 3$ convolution with stride 2 and padding 1. What is the final size?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\lfloor(n + 2p - k)/s\rfloor + 1$, twice.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Pooling: $\lfloor(64 - 2)/2\rfloor + 1 = 32$. Convolution: $\lfloor(32 + 2 - 3)/2\rfloor + 1 = 16$. So $16 \times 16$.
:::

---

**Q4.** What is the receptive field of four stacked $3 \times 3$ convolutions (stride 1, no pooling)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Each layer adds 2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$1 + 4 \cdot 2 = 9$ pixels: a $9 \times 9$ patch.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why are the layer-1 kernels of a trained network worth looking at as pictures, but the layer-3 kernels hardly?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does each kernel act on?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Layer-1 kernels act on pixels, so a kernel's picture is the image pattern it responds to (an edge, a line, a blob). Layer-3 kernels act on feature maps of layer 2: their weights mix abstract channels, and only the feature maps, the most exciting image patches or occlusion experiments show what such a unit responds to.
:::

---

**Q6.** You classify cells in microscope images whose orientation is arbitrary. Which augmentations would you use? Would you use the same for handwritten digits?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which changes keep the label?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Cells: rotations by any angle, flips, small shifts, brightness and contrast changes, a little noise. Digits: small rotations and shifts only. A 6 rotated by 180° is a 9, and a mirrored 2 or 7 is not a digit at all.
:::

---

**Q7.** *(math)* Two $3 \times 3$ convolutions without a nonlinearity in between. Show that they are one convolution, and give its size.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Convolution is associative.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(x * k_1) * k_2 = x * (k_1 * k_2)$: one kernel $k_1 * k_2$ of size $(3 + 3 - 1) \times (3 + 3 - 1) = 5 \times 5$. Without the ReLU, depth adds no new kind of function, only a larger linear filter (the collapse argument of the first unit, in convolutional form).
:::
